content: The prevalence of mental health and psychosocial problems in primary care settings is notably high. Counselling has been proposed as a potential treatment for these issues, but there is no clear consensus regarding its effectiveness in primary care environments. The objective of this review was to evaluate both the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of counselling for individuals with mental health and psychosocial problems in primary care settings. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of electronic databases was conducted, including the Cochrane Collaboration Depression, Anxiety and Neurosis (CCDAN) trials registers (up to December 2010), MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (up to May 2011). The review included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that specifically examined counselling interventions for mental health and psychosocial problems in primary care. Data extraction was performed using a standardised data extraction sheet by two independent reviewers. The quality of the included trials was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias criteria to determine the likelihood of systematic errors. Continuous outcome measures were analysed using standardised mean differences, and an overall effect size was calculated for each outcome with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Continuous data from different measurement tools were standardised by dividing mean values by standard deviations. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of the findings. Economic analyses were summarised narratively, but adverse events were not assessed. The review included nine trials with a total of 1,384 randomised participants. The studies varied in their risk of bias, with two trials identified as having a high risk of selection bias due to inadequate allocation concealment. All the included studies were conducted in primary care settings within the United Kingdom, ensuring a high level of comparability across the trials. The analysis revealed that counselling was significantly more effective than usual care in improving short-term mental health outcomes. The standardised mean difference for short-term mental health outcomes was -0.28 (95% CI: -0.43 to -0.13) based on data from six trials involving 772 participants. However, counselling did not demonstrate significant long-term benefits for mental health outcomes (standardised mean difference: -0.09, 95% CI: -0.27 to 0.10, based on four trials with 475 participants) or improvements in social functioning (standardised mean difference: -0.09, 95% CI: -0.29 to 0.11, based on three trials with 386 participants). Despite these findings, participants reported high levels of satisfaction with counselling. There was some evidence suggesting that the overall costs of counselling were comparable to those of usual care. However, there were limited data available for direct comparisons between counselling and other psychological therapies, medications, or psychosocial interventions. In conclusion, counselling was associated with significantly greater clinical effectiveness in improving short-term mental health outcomes compared to usual care. However, it did not provide additional benefits in the long term or in terms of social functioning. Participants expressed high satisfaction with counselling, but it did not appear to reduce overall healthcare costs. The applicability of these findings to settings outside the United Kingdom remains uncertain.
